People who are in the habit of reading the yob, court items in the Examiner" will have notic•el ' that every now and t there is a latch of olf•qiil- ers hauled bef, ore their betters' for having com- mitted the bi•inous iTilll4` of playing a gain, of chance with Isins -invariably copper ones. These sinful people are usually described as being youths,-or jav,riiii," and, Is n matter of fart. in nine cases our of ten they are ni•wsbuys gone wrong, in this one part Millar at least. The magis- trates, with the assumption of wisdom that seems generally to appertain to that exalt -I state of Into invariably treat ti,, .1.-liquen.s to a very •

VIRTrot'S MORAL LECTURE and end up by inflicting what is known as a 1111:11- 1.1 p•nalty. So recently as loot week a trio of coat ii. weretillacted by the Warrington magis- trates in thv Mal of ono shilling, each for having played aif ganw called tossing in the Eagle and yanl, and on the same occasion four young fellows were summoned and dealt with for hat mg : played pitch and toss in Rank-btreet. The et ilenee , given by the police in support at their east. indi- cated that these lads, or young men, exercised can- aiderable ingenuity in trying to carry on an'. unlaw- ful game- at such a way auto escape the 4etectp,o of the vigilant emissaries of the equally vi.,ihoo Chief Constable, awl if transpired t hat one of t defendants, who was on thiS OCCIViOII ordered to pay a tine of ten ohillings awl costs, had on a pre- vious occasion been in trouble for a similar offence,
TIIE EXCITEMENT THAT ATTRACTs.

Judging by thi,, and by similar cases, it would seem that the, gamblers in the humbler walks of life are not so much influenced by the possibility of making much gain as by the temporary diversion and excitement caused by awaiting the assue of the toss of a coin for, as the stakes played for are generally of the smallest possible value, it would he something approaching madness to run the risks of a magisterial line anu coeds for the sake of the possi- bility of coming off a few coppers to the good. To , tile it flown lea fine point, as to put it, it is the ex- • citement, and nothing but the excitement, that , brings victims into the meshes of the gambling net.
VICTIMS IN LAIIGIS NrIIIIERS.

These vecteen.,if they well excuse the ternuare even in Warrington to be numbered by their hundreds. but it is only, as a rule, the poorest of the poor that are compelle.l to publicly answer for their misdeeds. Trade speculation may in some instances be said to very closely approach the outer edges of the spirit of gambling. but apart from that there are very many respectable people in Warrington who see no! harm in risking a few odd shillings on the event of,! my, a horse race, a pigeon-Hying match. or a game at bowls or billiards. Disguise it as you like, gamb- ling is popular, both among the masses and the classes, from the aristocrat to the street urchin, and !I fear that it will continue to be so until the end of time.

div.head: ANCIENT GAIIELDE, PRECNIIENTE.
div.p: ANCIENT GAIIELDE, PRECNIIENTE.

..... ..... .. , .. The votaries of the pursuit have any amount of precedent. Deciding dispute., and acquiring pro- perty, by casting lots, and other forms of gam'''. mg, will be found referreel to in works of great antiquity. in the Bible we read of the selection of a king (Saul) by casting lots, and of a similar step prior to Jonah being east overboard as fomt for the fishes. Again, after the Crucifixion, " for His raiment they cast Iota" The ancient Ilindoo code vigorously denounces gambling, and it is reconled that the priests of Egypt, in order to bringone of their kings into exceptional disreputo, toll the people he PLAYED OATIES OF CHANCE IN THE INFERNAL

Cards were known t7l'l7e-Jilinese long before they were introducml into Europe. The Greenlanders , gamble with a board and a revolving linger-piece, while the African negro user shells as dice. Laws condemning high play were passed in times a long way hack, in various countries, but without mucli effect. In 1527 Latimer preached a sermon at Cambridge in which all the metaphont were based on card playing, and in the reign of the "Merry Cherie.; "a statute prohibiting the collection of heavy gambling debto woo passed.
I.`ROHHHTION THAT HIO NOT PHOHIBIT.

. ..... The indictment was heavy in appearance, but the remedy provided simply limited the amount of gambling debts that could be collected to _am Playing for cash NVEIS not prohibited, and Popp speaks of Lady Castlemaine losing .041.0 a al in one night's play. In subsequent reigns Parliaments passed various laws to check gaming, hut they were usually aimed more at tin, lower than the privileged classes. In the time of Henry VIII a law was passed prohibiting certain unlawful games to" all but gentlemen." History abounds with relations of incidents of high play and singular wagers, but during the last century there has been a consider- able lull in the fever of high play ao far as games at cards and dice are concerned, though iaerhaps " plunging' on horse raters has reached a higher tide than over before. ..,.OARBLING CONTRACTS ILLCOA

... In NU an Act was named tanking all contract% by way of gaming or wagering, null and void, anti pmviding that no suit should he maintainable in any Court "of law or equity to recover any sum of money or valuable thing alleged to have been won upon any wager, or which should have been de- • posited in tile hand, of any person to await an event ; on which atty wager should have been made." But the Act, delimit it gild much by making wagers in. capable of legal enforcement, did less to discourage gambling than a change int he attitude of those who had influence on the habits of English society. Play grew into disfavour, not only at Court, but among the ranks of statesmen and men of wealth and culture, and at the pn.sent day heavy gambling ! is pretty ninch confined to the turf; except in a few instances like those brought to light in Ismdon this week. Whist is played largely, and ati times for high stakes. but with thin exception there is comparatively little card-playing. Dice are only used in conjunction with the harmless backgammon board.
THE IGIVISLOPHICNN OF. HORSE RACING.

There ion gond deal of hotting on varions kinds of sport, hut all sinks into insig ii Name., beside the amount, of speculation on horse-raeing, the recent development of which has been enormous. Parlia- ments, acting on the view that horse-raring improves the !weed of horses, have looked with a lenient view on the matter, and now the professional betting : man has become an institution. Handicaps have : come into vogue ; short, elktallett nets are popular: Ismail meetings abound and there has sprang up powerful ring of proft salon.] bettors, whose business Is Inlay against any horse, and with all comers. . state. motion in favour M the ilisestabban- uncut of the English Church in Wales. As was ten be expected, the motion was rejcsited, but it may be taken as in sign of progress that the majority against it was :id only. The discussion turned largely 111011 the strength of Dissenters in Wales as eornpared with Churehmen ; and them was not I a little Id esentlicting, testimony. It is suggestive that Sir JOSEPH BAILEY, who spoke against the ani dim,. admitted that the Nonconformists in Wales were as two to one. How absurd then, ts gin no further, to talk of the Church of England being the Notional Church of Wales ! If Sunday School it &sties taken as a guide, it is found that the IM:senders in attendance as compamd with Church- , mon are as seven tin two. Then again no loss than fi ;I sills of the Parliamentary representa- tires of Wales are inn favour of disestablishment. As bearing miins this, it is interesting tin remember that bird DEnuv. who is an authority amongst Unionists. has laid it ilows that—" The question at ,oaintaining or disestablishing the Welsh Church I it. one whieh ought to be decided in actstrdanot wan the wishes if the Welsh people whenso- ever the:r wishes are authoritatively declared." App!yin4 this principle, and there is no denying its soundness from a democratic standpoint, the nse for disestahlishinent in Wales may be said to use in,rfe,t. But it is argued thud the Stints Church in Wales is really a part of the English Church, anal Parliament cannot disestablish one withod iltsestablishing the other. Mr. BYRON ItKED, who took the Church under Ins pride, , Lion. sahl—" Both parts of the island must, in reg nrl n the Established Church, be dealt with as one and indivisable, and it was therefore not ' , effic'ent, in order to justify this motion, to show tint the C'inroli was a failure in Wales. In order : to entice I.ut a case for itsdisestablishment it must ' be proved that it was not an good institution for I England Mid Wales taken together." Perlin); ment will probably make short work of this : difficulty when the Liberals are returned to power ; Ind, for all that, we rather like this view of the question. We have a strong opin- ion, apart from any question of numbers either one way or One other, that the alliance of Church and State is an unholy alliance ; that the State exercises an improper function when it pro- vides an religion for the people ; that no Church can be healthy. worldly or spiritually, which is
sailer the coi-itr,A of the Stat.O ; and that it is

tyranny to tax people, either directly or indirectly, for thesupport of a particular creed. Holding these views, we should like to see the whole question fought out on grounds broad enough to cover Disestahlishment awl Disendowment in England and S,othind as well as in Wales. But Englishmen move slowly, and they have is way of dealing with a pressidg grievance rather than of acting on logiod lines. The chances are that we shall, first, have Disestabliahment and Disendowment in Wales ; that Scotland will he the next country to be net free; and that there will boa long and hard fight for the separation of Church and State in England. However, if Mr. Braox Reno, an repre- senting the Church Defence Association, will only stick to his text, and insist upon England and Wales being dealt with as one Church, we shall be ver, pleased to assist hum—in our own way.

If the London Police did not wore in running down " Jack the Ripper," they made a palpable hit in their raid, on Sunday morning, upon the gambling dens of the metropolis. They were " mighty impartial " tin, ; they canght the big fish of the " Field " as well as the little fish of the " Adelphi." There were common men, and noble- men : and how noble they looked nest day at the Felice Court !

' Sir James Sawyer has followed the example of Mr. Rowlands, the chairman of the Executive Committee of the Birmingham Conservative Association ; he has resigned his position as President of the Association. He says :—"I find myself unable to hold office in our association because I could not again trust the Imulers of the Liberal Unionist party in Birmingham." Quite right keep it up. When Unionists fall out, Liberals will leave a chanty of gutting their own again.

WARNS and Co., exceedingly useful. : The title it bears is " How we are Governed," and ,t was written originally by ALBANY DE FON.. Ng,. ti the form of a series of letters. That, however,: :s so long since, and so many changes have taken • .1 in the meantime, that the work as now pre- ! e..t0l to the public has been entirely re-written • y Pie present editor -Mr. W. J. GORDON. It is .-.,eerbially difficult to &rota thorough understand-1 mg the British Constitution, AA it is not, like :natitutions, a creation—it is a growth. But the 11,,ndbook in question paves the way admirably. Archdcsicon Lefroy has been talking pretty plainly this week to churchwardens and sidemen ; he has been stirring them up. He does not behove in them raising funds for the church, as they have done at Winwiek, by "ten parties, halls, Ac. "Let them imagine,- he says, "St. Timothy arranging a ball to meet the expenses of the Clumb of Ephems!" Very good, but why not go a little further :nut try to imagine St. Timothy as an Arehdeacon with a fixed income, and no small one : or, better still, "housing the show " as an Archbishop with £lO,OOO a year !

The Arclekicon of Montgomery, the Von. D. R. Thomas, has been "warning " the people of Oswestry of the sudden and violent deaths that have taken place amongst anti-tithe agitators. He thinks the Almighty is on the side of tithes, and thus punishes those who object to them. Some years m mary party wore attacked and killed at Thal. del Fuego while in the act of prayer. Was this a " warning " against prayer? The Venerable Archdeacons was born in the wrong clime; in this country he is looked on as "a sport." Africa should have been his native wild where he might have frightened ignorant negroes, with his Mumbo-Jumbo. It won't do here.

Mr. Osborne Morgan —said a good many good things in his speech in the House of Commons on Tuesday, on Welsh disestablishment. He made a neat allusion to the raid on the gamblers thus : " There was no part of the United Kingdom in which the places f worship were so toll sum Wales, and there was no place whore the gaols were so empty. He remembered not so long ago, in three counties in Wales there was only one prisoner, and he was an Englishman. (Laughter). There was no country where the amusements were so pure PS in Wales. The Welsh did not go to prize- fights and gambling hens ; they left that to the , peers of the realm. (Laughter. r

div.p: BUENLEY GAZETTE, February 23rd.

UHE lot of those who toil from day to day in the bowels of the earth is not a very agreeable one. Apart from the terrible risks of which we are so often retninded by a calamitous explosion, with all its thrilling scenes, the collier has to pursue his work at . _ _

times under circumstances of great hardship. Mr. Moses Knowles, of 109, Oxford Road, Burnley, has had some experience of the trying iditions of labour in some of the deeper coal mines of this country. He relates he has repeatedly had to work for hours crouched in ten or twelve inches of water and the r.old liquid at the same time dropping all over his body from above. Happily such conditions of employment are almost unknown in the Burnley district, but Mr. Knowles has had to encounter them in other mining localities, and has been a painful !.(.1: in consequence. He first commenced with pains in his which gradually extended to other parts of the body.' " I low," said Mr. Knowles, " that I was obliged to be covered h blankets and have a chair close to the fire even on a wan,

div.head: WITH
div.p: WITH

lay. It was only then.that I could feel anything like warmth. My legs got so weak that I ;Ind to have the help of a stick to get across the floor. I was terribly troubled with indiges- tion, nervous debility, and disease of the liver and kidneys, and had constant attacks of cramp in the stomach. For many weeks I suffered dreadfully, writhing in agony for Lours together, and got so weak that it was painful to speal,, let alone trying to leave. ledicine only seemed to make me worse, and I iot so that my friends gave me up and the doctor ventured to offer no hope of a cure. At last I read one of 'Warner's pamphlets, sent for a bottle of `Warner',-- , Cure,' and oh ! how much good it did me. In a few weeks t was a - new man. My appetite returned, the weakness yeared, and I went back to my work feeling stronger than I had .lone for years." •

. .... The work of ;kis section is rapidly advancing. The railway embankments an. being, pushed forward and the future course"( the bind. and North Western Railway is clew ly discernible. The kwks by the hospital are having their due share .4 aztention. The stcam navvy is dis- pensed with on the last lift And tic work is carried on by the use of hall a dozen crancsdo whichia attached a huge bucket. At Wildegrave, the river diversion lanes, completion, and there are talks of letting the water in some time during the coming week. The large slip at Warburton is untouched. But gold work is being done at this end of the seetkm also, and the steam navvy is : clearinz the last course. The men are busy chipping ! down the dike; and any one who has regularly visited the wmks cannot fail to see that ni time is wasted. The night shitt has been dispensed with for some time; but the nom work a turn and quarter each day. So that little is k .st in that direction.
LATCHFORD LOCKS,

Latchford Station will be demolished when the new line is built, and a new station erected some distance away on the high enalainkinent. A walk along the section may or commenced there. The cutting into the yellow sand deepens till it eats into ref core of sandstone, and widens, too, to an extent which is not equalled on the whole course of the canal from Ea.stham. The magnitude of this gap in the earth is a necessity. Here is the site of the Latchfonl Loeks, the feat obstacle or. the Canal after a smooth sail of 21 miles from I:Radiant. There will be two siarelled locks of different sins for vessels of different tonnage the larger 0.500. long by 65ft. wide and the smaller 350 b. by 451 t. The sides of the cutting creep closer together as we pursue our journey. The din gets livelier, and we cons upon a considerable village called the

It is one of those .ttlements that suddenly rose upon the fields with mushroom growth at the bidding of the eonttactor, to blokes the plain for a few seasons, and then vanish, having not a wrack behind. An inspection is always worth the trouble. All the ministering indus- tries the engineer summons to his aid have each its allotted space—the carpenter's, the blacksmith's, the painters, and all the rest. One huge shed is the Told wherein are gathered at nights the engines which run about the cutting all day another, where the black- smiths work, is lit up with flickering furnace glows ; a third is filled with the pungent odour of paints and varnishes ; a fourth, strewn with shavings, shelters the hammering joiners ; a fifth is a big stable, and soon. The offices of the agent, Mr. J. Price, are more com- modious mete, omplete than usual, and contain the central apparatus of the telephone system between Manchester and Flotsam. There are several

STOVETS OF NAVVMS ACTS, with spacious back yard. The visitor can be shown a school where 100 children are taught, a mission hall as big as many &village church, and some distance away, a large hospital of two storeys, whenin tended pati- ents from the four sections bet ween Runcorn and Flar- ton. Not far from Thelwall yard the cutting stops. In front the Mersey trim the way. Within a very short distance it mews the line ,d the Canal twice. This is one of those loons the Mersey Sfqll6 down (eon the left, through which the Canal will have to bi cut. Tentii,r- ary bridges at present CT,m, the water, but very soon the channel will be wholly on the left.

TEA MEETING AT THELIVALL. On Tuesday evening the teaehers and a few friends hilonging to the Sabbath School cormivtod with the Mission Hall had their quarterly tea. This is one of the largest Sunday Schools on the Canal works, the average attendance being florin 125 to 130. Mr. 1/1.111,11, in the unavoidable absence of Mr. Price, agent, who is at Barry, took the chair. The evening was very pleas- antly spent. Mrs. Jenkins, Mrs. Darbyshire, and Mi. Bushell presided at the tea tables, and the following pro- gramme was gone through after the tea :—Mr. Stewart. address ; Mr. Rigby, recitation; Mr. Silverton, song ; Mr. Bushell. reading ; Mr. Rigby, tong; Miss Bushell. sang; Mr. Price, song; Miss Priestley, tong; Mr. John- son, song ; Mr. Bushell, reading; Miss Price, song ; Mr. Silverton, tong; Mr. Jenkins, address. Mr. Jenkins, in his address,tlianked the teachers fire their valued services during the past three months. He knew they had many discouragements and that the conduct of the children was not all that they could hope for. But as teachers they were to seek to make them totter; and in days and years to come the children who were sown, trouble- some would look back with glad'sao to the days when they sat under tireir care in tire Sunday School. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded tir Mr. Bushell for kin great kindness in taking the chair, and for the two roofings which he gave during the evening.

The dwellers near -WaCL:ZrII a 1,:‘; miles south-east of Warrington are being gradually accustomed to a new bdragraphy. An absent li.wth Cheshire man would hardly know his native heath if he were to come back when die Ship Canal is finished. Even now he would marvel much and rub Imb eyes at the change. Hardly anywhere on tho whole rse of the Canal is there suck a wholesale annihilation of e old landmarks, and such an erection of new ones, As on Ow section between Latch- ford and IbAlins Green, a distance of about live eat.,. A consider able river—the Mersey—is being led into anew course ; a long and lofty railway embankment is being raised like a huge wall between two parts of the lands- cape ; and roads that have never knowna canopynave the overhanging trees will soon he arched over with bridges. In this particular district the Mersey meanders very eccentrically, as if its desires was to tie itself in a knot. Five timow d,ao it croon the line of the Ship Canal. throwing big loops north and south of it. The southern I. daps will be eau oft altogether, end the river will par- taco straighter course on the north side. From near the middle 1.1 this section right along to the contlunne of the Mersey and he Irewell, and straight up the Irwell Is that Manchester docks, we shall have an enlarged and straightonnl canalised nver without a bend—a broad, noble Ship Canal, whose waters will stretch Iwtwasea stone enztrankments, instead of a crooked stream, lazily crawling along in placid contentment with its muddy banks.

div.head: OLD DISSENTING CHAPELS IN LANCASHIRE. BY THE REV. B. NIOUTINGALE.
div.p: OLD DISSENTING CHAPELS IN LANCASHIRE. BY THE REV. B. NIOUTINGALE.
-NONCONFORMITY IS WARRINGTON. CAIRO-STREET CHAPEL.

On the death of the Rev. Robert Yates, his son Samuel was chosen to succeed him by the Non- conformists of Warrington. lie was trained by the Rev. Richard Prankland, at Rathmell, entering there August 23rd, 1673. It is interesting to note that this was the year when the licenses of 1672 were withdrawn, and persecution again broke out against Dissenters; also that his college companion was Timothy Jollie, son of that staunch Nonconformist worthy, the Rev. Thomas Jollie, ejected from Al- them. anti afterwards minister at Wymondhouses, near Clitheroe. Of Mr. damsel Yates but little is known. According ton tablet in the chapel giving a list of ministers with slates of settlement and termination of ministry, Inc was at Warrington from 16754 to 1679. On Whitt authority the statement rests Ido not know all that 1 know is that he wan dead before 1696. Nor do we know how long they continued to worship in the old Court House, or when the tirst chapel was built. The Unitarian ' Pocket Almanac gives the three dates 1672, 1703, ' 1745. which respectively stand for the date of tine ! license of Court House, date of erection of first I chapel, and date of erection of second or present chapel. Mr. Samuel Yates was followed by the

REV. PETER ASPINWALL, who, like his predecessor, must be dismissed in a sentence or two. Ile was ejected from !lesion in Lancashire, afterwards coming to Warrington though the exact date of the beginning of his ministerial duties here is not known. On the 27th of September, 1092, an ordination service was held at KnutsfonLtheonlainers being Messrs. Risley,Cromp- ton, Angier, Bradshaw, Aspinwall and Ainsworth. Mr. Aspinwall preached on the occasion from Rom. x. 15. Ile stied at Warrington in 1696, and of his death there is the following notice in the Northow- ram Registers--" Mr. Aspinwall. N.C. [Non-cona- formitul minister, at Warrington, dyed June, 1690, 'aged 60." Following him in 1696 is the

REV. CHARLES OWEN, D.D. A remarkable character, and worthy of a lengthy notice. He was one of nine children, his father being John Owen of Bryn in the parish of Abernant near Carmarthen. Both father and mother are said to have been" zealous Church people, and yet their large family of nine children became all decided and conscientious Non-conformists ;—of whom three— David, James, and Charles--were ministers." David Owen was pastor of the church at Mennen, Carman henshire, from 1690 to 1710, dying there on the 7th of October, in that year at the age of 59 years. James Owen was born Nov. 1,1654, at Bryn. He spent his early ministerial years in different lons of Wales," but his usefulness in a short time so excited the rage of persecutors that his friends, within shoot nine months after his coming among them, in order to save his valuable life, thrught advisable to convey him by night to Bronycludwr, in Merionethshire, the residence of the excellent Hugh Owen." In 1670 he became chaplain to Mrs. Baker.of Swiney, near Oswestry. preaching also ton "congregation of serious people in and about Oswestry." In Nov. 17th 1079 lie was married at Oswestry to Mrs. Sarah George, by whom he had seven children, two only of whom survived him. ' In 1696 he was invited to Manchester, but declined and removed ifl 1700 to Shrewsbury.. Here besides attending to his pastoral duties. he educated several young men for the ministry. He died from stone brought on by incessant application to literary pursuits on the Bth of April. 1706. aged 52 years; and was buried at St. Chad's, Shrewsbury. His ' funeral sermon was preached by Matthew Henry, from Arts so. 38. Ile war the author of several works of a theological and polemical character, amongst them being two or three interims relating to Parson Gipps, of Bury, anti Ilk animadversions against dissenters. Charles Owen was the youngest !of the three brothers,and as already stated succeeded the Rev. P. Aspinwall, at 'Farrington, in 1690. , Early in his ministry the first meeting house was erected on the site of the present one. According to Or. Evans's list of Presbyterian chapels drawn up between the years 1717 and 1729 it had a congregation of 71$ persons of whom 82 were county voters, and was by far the largest and most important dissenting congregation in this division of Lanca.him. Or. Charles Owen is des- erilied ass "preacher, a scholar, and a patriot." During the rebellion of 1715 several of the liissPnt- ing ministers in Lancashire laid aside their wearsins spiritual for weapons carnal, and marched with their rongregations against the advancing rebels. The Revs. James Woods, of Chowbent, John Walker of Horwich, and John Turner, of Preston, am particularly named in contemporary documents for their military exploits." Dr. Halley says that Dr. Owen defended the rights of King George as zealously and boldly with his pen as James Woods, of Chowbent, did with his pitchfork.- lliodoirsg so brought him into serious trouble. Some of his statements respecting his Royalist neighbours were deemed libellous, and though, as Dr. Halley says, "he obtained an acquits!, the expense of the pro- ceedings was almost as ruinous as if he hail been convicted and sentenced to pay heavy damages." I Ile was the author of a considerable number of pamphlets and sermon tracts which were "in good repute for some years after his death." After a , ministry of about fifty years. in Warrington he died in February. 1740. His funeral sermon was preached oath." 23rd of that month by his nephew; the Rev. James Owen of Rochdale. Or. Owen lived ! to see the need of a new building for his congre- gation which was erected in 1745. Concerning this

Mrs. Stead had been living apart from him, but hail returned, and sane dispute arose. After being . convicted he entered into a deed of separation, and allowed his wife £4 a week for the support of herself and the children. On Friday last he was eitargisl before the Widnes magistrates with wounding Churl's Wehtter, a teamsman in his employ, by striking him violently on the head with a walking stick, :mil was committed to the Liverpool Amiws, bail being allowed: This seemed to have had considerable effect upon his mind, and he has since been peeuliar in his manner. About fiveieclock on Tuesday night he went to his bedroom while Mrs. : Wilson, his housekeeper, was preparing tint. A report ! of fin-arias was heard, and on Mrs. Wilson proceeding ' upstairs a shocking spectacle was witnessed by her. Mr. Stead bad taken a doublmbarnillist gun, said placed his garter under his foot. Ile then tied it to the trigger and plaeoil the barrel to his head as he sat on the Issl. Ile hail then extended his leg, and the gun was discharged. : Su violent was the shock that the greater part of his load was blown away, and the room was strewn with his brains and portions of the skull. An alarm was raised, and Constable Foster was called. Dr. t.ivso'y,stf Farnworth, was soon in attendance, but could not, of course, render any assistance, as death hail hien instantaneous. Mr. A. Browne, solicitor, of Warrington, who hail &tenths! Mr. Stead Litton' the Widnes magi. trate+, was also summoned, and the coroner was corns umnicatisl with tlimugh Mr. Superintendent Johnston, if Whines.
